integrated_multimodal_description: [Shot 1] Live-action, deliberately overdramatic early-2000s romantic-comedy movie trailer titled "SEX AND THE CITY GOES TO MARS." Carrie Bradshaw and Samantha Jones are the only principal characters. Carrie Bradshaw has shoulder-length curly blonde hair, a slim figure, glamorous makeup, and wears an extravagant designer-style silver space suit with fashionable high-heeled space boots and a transparent bubble helmet. Samantha Jones has shoulder-length blonde hair, glamorous makeup, and wears a fitted metallic-gold designer-style space suit with matching boots and a transparent bubble helmet. They stand together inside an absurdly luxurious pink-and-silver spacecraft approaching MARS, with the enormous red planet filling the windows. A deep, gravelly male movie-trailer narrator (S1) says in an off-screen voiceover: <d>[English] This summer... two women are going where no Manhattan socialite has gone before.</d> while Carrie and Samantha's lips remain completely closed. [Shot 2] At 00:06.000, the camera cuts to Carrie and Samantha dramatically walking down the spacecraft ramp onto the dusty red surface of Mars. Their fashionable boots immediately sink awkwardly into the Martian dirt. Carrie looks down at her boots in horror. Carrie Bradshaw, with a sophisticated adult female voice (S2), says: <d>[English] Samantha, these boots are ruined.</d> [Shot 3] At 00:11.000, the camera cuts to Samantha standing beside Carrie beneath the enormous Martian sky. Samantha examines the completely barren landscape and gestures at the rocks surrounding them. Samantha Jones, with a confident adult female voice (S3), says: <d>[English] Forget the boots. Where are all the men?</d>

overall_soundscape: Spaceship engines and electronic controls transition into the muffled mechanical hiss of an airlock, metallic ramp movement, boots sinking into Martian soil, light suit movement, and a persistent artificial life-support hum.

non_diegetic_music: Oversized romantic-comedy trailer music with dramatic orchestral strings, electronic drums, glossy synthesizer accents, and a large brass flourish as Mars is revealed.

Carrie Bradshaw has shoulder-length curly blonde hair, a slim figure, glamorous makeup, and wears an extravagant designer-style SILVER SPACE SUIT with fashionable high-heeled space boots and a transparent bubble helmet. Both women stand on the dusty red surface of MARS beside their luxurious pink-and-silver spacecraft. The barren landscape contains red rocks, distant mountains, craters, and absolutely no other people. At the EXACT BEGINNING, Samantha is still looking around the empty landscape after asking where all the men are. A deep, gravelly male movie-trailer narrator (S1) says in an off-screen voiceover: <d>[English] They came looking for adventure...</d> while Carrie and Samantha's lips remain completely closed. [Shot 2] At 00:04.000, the camera cuts to Carrie and Samantha trudging across the red desert. Carrie struggles to walk in her ridiculous high-heeled space boots. She stops and stares down at the Martian dust covering them. Carrie Bradshaw, with a sophisticated adult female voice (S2), says: <d>[English] I hate Mars. The footing is terrible.</d> [Shot 3] At 00:09.000, the camera cuts to Samantha climbing onto a rock and scanning the horizon. Samantha Jones, with a confident adult female voice (S3), says: <d>[English] No restaurants. No cocktails. No men.</d> [Shot 4] At 00:13.000, a distant Martian rover suddenly drives over a ridge. Carrie and Samantha simultaneously turn toward it as dramatic sunlight silhouettes the approaching vehicle.

overall_soundscape: Constant spacesuit life-support hum, boots crunching through Martian soil, occasional wind-like suit vibration, rocks shifting beneath their feet, and the distant mechanical rumble of an approaching rover.

non_diegetic_music: Glossy romantic-comedy trailer score with rhythmic strings, electronic percussion, bright synthesizers, and an exaggerated orchestral swell when the mysterious rover appears.

integrated_multimodal_description: [Shot 1] Live-action, deliberately overdramatic early-2000s romantic-comedy movie trailer titled "SEX AND THE CITY GOES TO MARS." Carrie Bradshaw has shoulder-length curly blonde hair, a slim figure, glamorous makeup, and wears an extravagant designer-style SILVER SPACE SUIT with fashionable high-heeled space boots and a transparent bubble helmet. Samantha Jones has shoulder-length blonde hair, glamorous makeup, and wears a fitted METALLIC-GOLD SPACE SUIT with matching boots and a transparent bubble helmet. Both women stand together on the dusty red surface of MARS surrounded by red rocks, distant mountains, and craters. Their luxurious pink-and-silver spacecraft is visible far behind them. At the EXACT BEGINNING, Carrie and Samantha are staring toward a Martian rover that has just appeared over a distant ridge. The rover rapidly approaches them through clouds of red dust. A deep, gravelly male movie-trailer narrator (S1) says in an off-screen voiceover: <d>[English] But sometimes... finding yourself means leaving the entire planet.</d> while Carrie and Samantha's lips remain completely closed. [Shot 2] At 00:06.000, the rover stops beside them. Its hatch opens dramatically. Carrie and Samantha eagerly lean forward, expecting someone glamorous to emerge. Instead, a tiny NASA exploration robot rolls out and mechanically scans them. Samantha's expression collapses. Samantha Jones, with a confident adult female voice (S3), says: <d>[English] I'm going back to Manhattan.</d> [Shot 3] At 00:11.000, the camera cuts extremely wide as Carrie and Samantha march back toward their spacecraft while the tiny rover follows them. Carrie struggles through the dust in her high-heeled space boots. Giant glittering movie-trailer lettering fills the Martian sky: "SEX AND THE CITY GOES TO MARS." The deep male narrator (S1) says in an off-screen voiceover: <d>[English] Coming soon... unfortunately.</d> while Carrie and Samantha's lips remain completely closed.

overall_soundscape: Martian soil crunches beneath their boots, the rover motor whines, mechanical servos move, the spacecraft hums in the distance, and the women's suits produce subtle life-support and fabric sounds.

non_diegetic_music: Bombastic romantic-comedy trailer music with sweeping strings, glossy synthesizers, electronic drums, triumphant brass, and an excessively large orchestral ending beneath the final title.

nodes.title: Prompt Skill.MD (Built for Reference System)
widgets_values:
==================================================

FULL-REFERENCE VIDEO PROMPT SKILL

==================================================

This skill generates structured MiniMax full-reference video prompts.

All prompts use ONE unified reference system.

There is NO separate built-in-character reference system.

Legacy reference formats such as:

^Character Name^

~Character Name~

are NOT used.

All supplied characters, including known television, film, celebrity, original, or user-provided characters, use the SAME unified character-reference system:

Visual reference:

{Character_Name}

Voice reference:

§Character_Name§

The workflow may internally expand these reference tokens into detailed visual or audio reference information.

==================================================

REFERENCE SYSTEM — CRITICAL

==================================================

REFERENCE TAGS ARE WORKFLOW REFERENCE TOKENS.

They are NOT ordinary character names.

A supplied reference such as:

{George_Costanza}

may be expanded or replaced by the workflow with detailed visual-reference information such as:

George Costanza played by Jason Alexander on Seinfeld

Likewise:

§George_Costanza§

may be expanded or replaced with detailed voice-reference information such as:

voice of Jason Alexander performing George Costanza on Seinfeld

Because of this behavior, reference tags must be used deliberately.

A REFERENCE TAG invokes or reinforces a workflow reference.

A PLAIN NAME merely refers to the already-established character in ordinary descriptive prose or spoken dialogue.

==================================================

UNIFIED CHARACTER REFERENCE SYSTEM

==================================================

Every referenced speaking character uses:

Visual reference:

{Character_Name}

Voice reference:

§Character_Name§

Example input:

{George_Costanza}

Voice: §George_Costanza§

Image: George Costanza played by Jason Alexander in Seinfeld

Voice: voice of Jason Alexander as George Costanza in Seinfeld

The visual reference and voice reference are DIFFERENT workflow tokens.

They MUST both be preserved exactly when invoked.

Visual:

{George_Costanza}

Voice:

§George_Costanza§

NEVER substitute one for the other.

==================================================

HARD CHARACTER MAPPING RULE

==================================================

Every speaking character follows:

{Character_Name} → §Character_Name§

Example:

{George_Costanza}

must use:

§George_Costanza§

for the character's voice reference.

CORRECT:

{George_Costanza} (S1) says, <d>[English §George_Costanza§]I'm getting upset!</d>

WRONG:

{George_Costanza} (S1) says, <d>[English George_Costanza]I'm getting upset!</d>

WRONG:

{George_Costanza} (S1) says, <d>[English {George_Costanza}]I'm getting upset!</d>

WRONG:

George Costanza (S1) says, <d>[English §Jerry_Seinfeld§]I'm getting upset!</d>

Whenever a supplied reference tag is invoked, preserve it EXACTLY.

Never replace, rename, normalize, escape, omit, or alter the contents or symbols of an invoked reference token.

The characters:

< >

{

}

§

/

are meaningful syntax when used in reference or dialogue tags and MUST survive exactly in generated output.

Legacy:

^

~

reference syntax must NOT be generated.

==================================================

REFERENCE INVOCATION VS ORDINARY CHARACTER MENTION

==================================================

A reference token INVOKES the corresponding workflow reference.

A plain human-readable name merely MENTIONS the already-established character.

These are intentionally different operations.

Example:

{George_Costanza} sits on the sofa.

This invokes and reinforces George's supplied visual reference.

After George is clearly established:

George turns toward Jerry.

This is allowed.

The second sentence refers to the SAME established physical character without invoking the reference again.

Likewise:

{Cosmo_Kramer} enters through the apartment door.

Kramer points toward the kitchen.

This is allowed.

Reference tokens should be used enough to establish and reinforce identity, but they DO NOT need to replace every occurrence of a character's name.

Ordinary names are especially useful:

* in natural descriptive prose

* inside spoken dialogue

* when another character verbally mentions someone

* when repeated reference expansion would be unnecessary

* when the physical identity is already unambiguous

A plain-name mention NEVER creates a second physical instance of an already-established character.

==================================================

ABSOLUTE RULE — VISUAL REFERENCE TAGS INSIDE SPOKEN DIALOGUE

==================================================

VISUAL REFERENCE TAGS MUST NEVER APPEAR IN THE ACTUAL SPOKEN WORDS.

This includes:

{Character_Name}

{Location_Name}

{Object_Name}

{Vehicle_Name}

{Creature_Name}

or any other visual workflow-reference token.

Visual reference tokens may be expanded by the workflow.

If one is placed inside spoken dialogue, the expanded reference information may become part of what the character attempts to say aloud.

WRONG:

{George_Costanza} (S1) says, <d>[English §George_Costanza§]{Jerry_Seinfeld} doesn't understand me.</d>

CORRECT:

{George_Costanza} (S1) says, <d>[English §George_Costanza§]Jerry doesn't understand me.</d>

WRONG:

{Jerry_Seinfeld} (S1) says, <d>[English §Jerry_Seinfeld§]Let's go to {Monks_Coffee}.</d>

CORRECT:

{Jerry_Seinfeld} (S1) says, <d>[English §Jerry_Seinfeld§]Let's go to the coffee shop.</d>

When a character verbally mentions another referenced entity, use its NORMAL HUMAN-READABLE NAME.

==================================================

VOICE TOKENS INSIDE DIALOGUE

==================================================

The speaking character's VOICE TOKEN is REQUIRED inside the dialogue header.

Format:

[English §Character_Name§]

Example:

{Cosmo_Kramer} (S2) says, <d>[English §Cosmo_Kramer§]I've got an idea!</d>

The voice token is metadata selecting the speaker's voice.

It is NOT part of the literal spoken sentence.

Everything after the closing:

]

and before:

</d>

represents words the character literally says aloud.

==================================================

DIALOGUE TAG PRESERVATION — ABSOLUTE

==================================================

EVERY spoken line MUST be wrapped in literal opening and closing dialogue tags:

<d>

</d>

These tags are REQUIRED OUTPUT SYNTAX.

They are NOT optional formatting.

NEVER strip, escape, convert, summarize, or omit:

<d>

</d>

Every opening:

<d>

MUST have exactly one matching:

</d>

Only spoken words and required language/voice metadata belong inside:

<d>...</d>

Actions, expressions, camera directions, descriptions, reference invocations, sound effects, and location references MUST remain outside the dialogue tags.

==================================================

FULL-REFERENCE LABEL SYSTEM

==================================================

Every prompt uses full-reference labels to track visible and audio reference information.

The allowed labels are:

<Subject N>

<Picture N>

<Video N>

<Audio N>

==================================================

<Subject N>

==================================================

Use:

<Subject N>

for reusable visible content in the generated video.

This may include:

* characters

* locations

* objects

* creatures

* vehicles

* costumes

* visible effects

* environments

* other visible referenced content

Each independently tracked visible reference receives its own Subject number.

Example:

<Subject 1> is {George_Costanza}, George Costanza as defined by the supplied character reference, wearing a dark jacket, button-down shirt, dark trousers, and dark shoes.

<Subject 2> is {Jerry_Seinfeld}, Jerry Seinfeld as defined by the supplied character reference, wearing a casual button-down shirt, dark trousers, and sneakers.

<Subject 3> is {Jerry_Seinfeld_Apartment}, preserving the supplied apartment environment.

If the source reference already establishes appearance sufficiently, do not unnecessarily invent or repeat excessive physical details.

Add clothing, state, geography, or scene-specific details when useful for generation consistency.

==================================================

<Picture N>

==================================================

Use a standalone:

<Picture N>

ONLY when a supplied image itself serves as:

* a first-frame anchor

* last-frame anchor

* specific keyframe

* edited keyframe

* concrete composition anchor

* storyboard/planning image

If an image merely defines the appearance of a character, environment, prop, or other subject, do NOT create a separate Picture label.

Instead define the reference as a Subject.

==================================================

<Video N>

==================================================

Use:

<Video N>

only when a reference video has a whole-video role such as:

* direct video editing

* direct video continuation

* source-video temporal structure

* camera-motion reference

* cut structure

* pacing structure

A character or object appearing in a reference video is still represented as:

<Subject N>

when that visible content is reused.

Do not create <Video N> merely because a character reference happens to originate from video.

==================================================

<Audio N> — CRITICAL VOICE-SEPARATION RULE

==================================================

EVERY speaking referenced character receives an explicit independent:

<Audio N>

entry in:

subject_definitions:

This is a MAJOR voice-consistency rule.

Bind each Audio reference explicitly to BOTH:

1. the corresponding <Subject N>

2. the corresponding global speaker ID (Sx)

Example:

<Audio 1> is the voice-timbre reference for <Subject 1> (S1), using §George_Costanza§.

<Audio 2> is the voice-timbre reference for <Subject 2> (S2), using §Jerry_Seinfeld§.

<Audio 3> is the voice-timbre reference for <Subject 3> (S3), using §Cosmo_Kramer§.

When useful, describe the referenced performance:

<Audio 1> is the voice-timbre reference for <Subject 1> (S1), using §George_Costanza§: the voice of Jason Alexander performing George Costanza in Seinfeld.

A character who does NOT speak in the current prompt normally does NOT require an <Audio N> definition.

Audio numbers are independent of Subject numbers.

However, for clarity, when practical, define character audio references in the SAME order as the corresponding speakers.

==================================================

AUDIO REFERENCE PURPOSE

==================================================

The explicit Audio mapping exists to reduce:

* voice drift

* voice swapping

* character-to-voice confusion

* one character inheriting another character's timbre

* vocal identity changes after shot cuts

* multi-character dialogue ambiguity

Each speaker's audio reference applies ONLY to that speaker.

Example:

<Audio 1>: reference - only §George_Costanza§ voice timbre, cadence, and expressive delivery guide <Subject 1> (S1).

<Audio 2>: reference - only §Jerry_Seinfeld§ voice timbre, cadence, and conversational delivery guide <Subject 2> (S2).

Do not describe one Audio reference as controlling multiple speakers unless explicitly requested.

==================================================

MULTIPLE SPEAKERS ARE ALLOWED

==================================================

There is NO fixed two-speaker maximum.

Three or more distinct characters MAY speak inside the same prompt when requested or when natural for the scene.

Example:

S1 = George

S2 = Jerry

S3 = Kramer

Additional speakers may use:

S4

S5

and higher IDs when genuinely needed.

However, voice clarity remains more important than maximizing the number of speakers.

Use only as many speaking characters as the scene actually needs.

When multiple characters speak, enforce strict vocal separation using:

* independent <Audio N> mappings

* stable speaker IDs

* one character speaking at a time whenever possible

* isolated or clearly composed speaker shots

* explicit closed-mouth states for non-speakers

* no unnecessary overlapping speech

* clear completion of one turn before the next begins

==================================================

SPEAKER IDS — GLOBAL WITHIN EACH PROMPT

==================================================

Assign speaker IDs according to the order of the FIRST ACTUAL VOCAL EVENT in the target prompt.

First distinct speaker:

(S1)

Second distinct speaker:

(S2)

Third distinct speaker:

(S3)

Fourth distinct speaker:

(S4)

and so on.

Reuse the SAME speaker ID every time that character speaks during that prompt.

Speaker IDs reset at the beginning of every new prompt.

Example:

George speaks first:

<Subject 1> (S1)

Jerry speaks second:

<Subject 2> (S2)

Kramer speaks third:

<Subject 3> (S3)

If George speaks again later in the prompt, George remains:

(S1)

Do NOT renumber George based on later speaking order.

==================================================

VOICE ISOLATION — CRITICAL

==================================================

For every spoken turn, explicitly establish which speaker owns the current voice.

Preferred language:

Using only the voice identity referenced from <Audio 1>, <Subject 1> (S1) says, ...

Using <Audio 2> exclusively, <Subject 2> (S2) says, ...

Using only the energetic voice identity referenced from <Audio 3>, <Subject 3> (S3) says, ...

This language is especially useful when:

* three or more characters speak

* characters have similar voices

* previous generations showed voice drift

* speakers appear together in the frame

* dialogue alternates quickly

==================================================

NON-SPEAKERS DURING DIALOGUE — CRITICAL

==================================================

Whenever one character speaks, explicitly keep other visible characters silent when doing so improves reliability.

Useful language:

Jerry and Kramer remain completely silent with closed mouths.

George is off-camera and produces no vocal sound.

Kramer listens with his lips fully closed.

The other characters react silently.

No other character speaks during this line.

When practical, the upcoming speaker should NOT visibly mouth words during another speaker's dialogue.

==================================================

TURN-TAKING — CRITICAL

==================================================

Prefer one clearly completed vocal turn at a time.

Recommended sequence:

1. Speaker begins.

2. Speaker completes the entire sentence.

3. Speaker's lips close.

4. Speaker stops producing vocal sound.

5. Brief visual handoff.

6. Next speaker becomes visually active.

7. Next speaker begins speaking.

Useful wording:

George finishes the entire sentence and closes his mouth.

Jerry does not begin speaking until George's mouth is fully closed.

Kramer completes his line, closes his lips, and remains silent.

Then cut to Jerry before Jerry begins speaking.

Avoid unnecessary simultaneous dialogue.

Overlapping dialogue is permitted only when the user explicitly wants interruption, chaos, argument overlap, crowd speech, or another effect where overlap is important.

==================================================

ISOLATED SPEAKER SHOTS — RECOMMENDED

==================================================

When multiple referenced voices are used in one prompt, isolated speaker framing is strongly preferred for important lines.

Example:

[Shot 1]

Three-shot establishing everyone.

George speaks.

[Shot 2]

Isolated medium close-up of Jerry.

George and Kramer are off-camera and silent.

Jerry speaks.

[Shot 3]

Isolated medium shot of Kramer.

George and Jerry are off-camera and silent.

Kramer speaks.

This visual separation helps reinforce the connection between:

<Subject N>

(Sx)

<Audio N>

and the active visible mouth.

A three-shot or two-shot may still be used when composition or comedy benefits from it.

==================================================

LOCATIONS & OTHER REFERENCES

==================================================

Locations, objects, creatures, vehicles, environments, and other supplied visible references may use:

{Reference_Name}

These are workflow reference tokens.

Determine from context whether each reference represents:

* a speaking character

* a silent character

* a location

* an object

* a creature

* a vehicle

* another visual asset

Only speaking characters receive:

* speaker IDs

* character voice references

* corresponding <Audio N> voice definitions

A location such as:

{Jerry_Seinfeld_Apartment}

does NOT receive:

§Jerry_Seinfeld_Apartment§

unless it is explicitly established as a speaking entity.

==================================================

LOCATION CHANGES — ABSOLUTE HARD RULE

==================================================

A PHYSICAL LOCATION CHANGE MAY ONLY OCCUR AT THE BEGINNING OF A NEW PROMPT.

NEVER change physical locations in the middle of a 15-second prompt.

EVERY prompt takes place in exactly ONE physical location.

A prompt may contain:

* multiple camera angles

* cuts

* camera movement

* reframing

* character movement

* entrances

* exits

* movement between parts of the same room

but all shots MUST remain inside the SAME physical environment.

If the story requires another location:

1. Finish the current prompt entirely inside the current location.

2. End the current prompt normally.

3. Output the prompt separator:

|

4. Begin the NEXT prompt with:

[new_location]

5. Immediately after [new_location], begin:

subject_definitions:

EXACT STRUCTURE:

|

[new_location]

subject_definitions:

==================================================
